Calculate sample size per timepoint to detect a linear trend in prevalence

Source: R/design_trend.R
design_trend.Rd

Given the prevalence at the first timepoint and either the prevalence at the last timepoint or a slope, returns the number of people needed per timepoint to detect a linear trend with the target power, using the test in test_trend(). Supply n_per_timepoint instead to run it in reverse: the function then reports the power that number of people per timepoint gives. Every timepoint gets the same design.

Three design modes – controlled by n_sites and n_per_site, at each timepoint:

Unclustered (n_sites = NULL, n_per_site = NULL)

Returns the number of people per timepoint.

Fixed site size (n_per_site supplied)

Solves for the number of sites per timepoint.

Fixed number of sites (n_sites supplied)

Solves for the number of people per site.

Usage

design_trend(
  prevalence_start,
  prevalence_end = NULL,
  slope = NULL,
  n_timepoints = NULL,
  times = NULL,
  n_per_timepoint = NULL,
  power = 0.8,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  n_sites = NULL,
  n_per_site = NULL,
  icc = 0
)

Arguments

prevalence_start

Expected true prevalence at the first timepoint, in (0, 1).

prevalence_end

Expected true prevalence at the last timepoint, in (0, 1). Supply exactly one of prevalence_end and slope.

slope

Change in true prevalence per unit of time. Supply exactly one of prevalence_end and slope.

n_timepoints

Whole number, 2 or more: equally spaced timepoints 0, 1, ..., n_timepoints - 1. Supply exactly one of n_timepoints and times.

times

Numeric vector of at least two timepoints, for unequal spacing or real units (for example calendar years).

n_per_timepoint

Optional whole number. If supplied, the function runs in reverse and reports the power this many people per timepoint give; power is then not used.

power

Target power, in [0.5, 1); default 0.80.

alternative

Direction of the test, as used later in test_trend(): "two.sided" (default), "greater" (an increase) or "less" (a decrease).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1.

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1. sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level, in (0, 1); default 0.95. The significance level of the test is 1 - conf_level.

n_sites

Optional whole number. Fixes the number of sites per timepoint; the function solves for people per site. Cannot be used with n_per_site.

n_per_site

Optional whole number. Fixes the number of people per site; the function solves for the number of sites per timepoint. Cannot be used with n_sites.

icc

Intra-cluster correlation, in [0, 1]; default 0 (no clustering). An icc above 0 needs n_sites or n_per_site.

Value

A list with:

n_per_timepoint

People per timepoint (or as supplied, in reverse). With sites, n_sites * n_per_site.

n

Total over all timepoints.

n_sites

Sites per timepoint (NULL if unclustered).

n_per_site

People per site (NULL if unclustered).

deff

Design effect at each timepoint; 1 if unclustered.

n_eff

Unclustered people per timepoint \(n_0\), rounded up (in reverse, n_per_timepoint / deff).

power

The target (forward), or the power achieved (reverse).

Details

Sample size per timepoint. The test fits a straight line through the measured prevalences at times \(t_1, \dots, t_T\). With \(n\) people per timepoint, its slope has variance about \(\bar\sigma^2_{app} / (n S_{xx})\), where \(S_{xx} = \sum_i (t_i - \bar t)^2\) and \(\bar\sigma^2_{app} = \bar p_{app}(1 - \bar p_{app})\) uses the average of the first and last measured prevalences. Detecting a measured slope \(\beta_{app}\) with the target power needs

$$n_0 = \frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2 \, \bar\sigma^2_{app}} {S_{xx} \, \beta_{app}^2},$$

with \(z_\beta\) the normal quantile at power and \(z_\alpha\) at \(1 - \alpha/2\) (two-sided) or \(1 - \alpha\) (one-sided). The measured slope is the true slope times \(Se + Sp - 1\), so an imperfect test needs more people (Dupont & Plummer 1998).

Clustering, as in design_precision(): with n_per_site fixed, \(n = n_0 D_{eff}\) with \(D_{eff} = 1 + (n_{per site} - 1) ICC\); with n_sites fixed, \(n = n_0 n_{sites}(1 - ICC) / (n_{sites} - n_0 ICC)\), which exists only when \(n_{sites} > n_0 ICC\); otherwise the function stops and reports the highest power those sites can give. If fewer people are needed than there are sites, fewer sites are used, with 1 person at each, and a warning says so. With sites, n_per_timepoint is the number actually sampled, n_sites * n_per_site.

Reverse mode. The same equation run backwards: the power of the slope test with \(n / D_{eff}\) people per timepoint.

References

Dupont, W. D. & Plummer, W. D. (1998) Power and sample size calculations for studies involving linear regression. Controlled Clinical Trials 19(6), 589-601.

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley. (Design effect.)

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

See also

test_trend()

Examples

# Prevalence rising from 10 to 20 percent over 5 annual rounds
design_trend(prevalence_start = 0.10, prevalence_end = 0.20, n_timepoints = 5)
#> $n_per_timepoint
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 805
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8
#> 

# The same trend given as a slope
design_trend(prevalence_start = 0.10, slope = 0.025, n_timepoints = 5)
#> $n_per_timepoint
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 805
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8
#> 

# Reverse: the power of 150 people per round
design_trend(0.10, prevalence_end = 0.20, n_timepoints = 5,
             n_per_timepoint = 150)
#> $n_per_timepoint
#> [1] 150
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 750
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 150
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.7738757
#> 

# Fixed site size: how many sites per round?
design_trend(0.10, prevalence_end = 0.20, n_timepoints = 5,
             n_per_site = 25, icc = 0.03)
#> $n_per_timepoint
#> [1] 300
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 1500
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 12
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 25
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.72
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 161
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8
#>
